lesson.title: From Z to Probability: The Mechanics of Calculating a P-Value
lesson.summary: Calculating a p-value means finding the tail area, or areas, of the sampling distribution beyond your test statistic, and the exact recipe depends on whether the alternative hypothesis is one-sided or two-sided.
lesson.body:
The general mechanics have two steps. First, compute the test statistic z. Second, find the area under the standard normal curve that matches the direction of Ha. If Ha points "greater than," the p-value is P(Z greater than or equal to z), the area to the right of the test statistic. If Ha points "less than," the p-value is P(Z less than or equal to z), the area to the left. If Ha is two-sided, "not equal to," the p-value is 2 times P(Z greater than or equal to the absolute value of z), found by doubling the single tail area beyond the absolute value of the test statistic.

Walk through the cereal box example again with the arithmetic laid out explicitly. The test statistic was z = negative 2.00. From a standard normal table, the cumulative probability up to z = 2.00 is 0.9772, so the area beyond 2.00 in one tail is 1 minus 0.9772, which is 0.0228, and by symmetry that equals the area at or below negative 2.00. For a one-sided test with Ha: mu < 16, the p-value is just that single tail: p = 0.0228. For a two-sided test with Ha: mu is not equal to 16, the p-value doubles: p = 2 times 0.0228, which is 0.0456.

Now do the same bookkeeping for the coin example. The test statistic there was z = 2.40. The cumulative probability up to z = 2.40 is 0.9918, so the area beyond 2.40 is 1 minus 0.9918, which is 0.0082. For a one-sided test with Ha: p > 0.5, the p-value is that single tail: p = 0.0082. For a two-sided test with Ha: p is not equal to 0.5, the p-value doubles: p = 2 times 0.0082, which is 0.0164.

The most common arithmetic mistake is mismatching the doubling to the actual alternative hypothesis: doubling a one-sided test's p-value by habit, or forgetting to double a genuinely two-sided test. The fix is always the same, look back at how Ha was written down before the data were collected, and let that decide whether one tail or two tails belong in the calculation, the same discipline emphasized when the two-sided test was introduced. In practice you can find these tail areas from a printed standard normal table, as done above, or from a calculator or software's normal cumulative distribution function. The underlying logic is identical either way, technology just automates the table lookup.
